title: Bitcoin holds near $70,000 as investors watch oil prices, inflation data: CNBC Crypto World
transcript_text: This week, Bitcoin wrestles with the $70,000 mark, Binance sews the Wall Street Journal over alleged defamation, and Carlos Domingo of Securitize weighs in on new guidance from federal regulators around tokenized securities. Welcome to CNBC's Crypto World, I'm McKenzie Cigallos. Crypto markets are in the red of the last week, as investors receive mixed signals on when the Iran conflict went. As of New New Eastern, Bitcoin tried to hold on to that $70,000 level, a benchmark that had also hit last week. Over the course of the past seven days, the flagship cryptocurrency was down more than 4%. Meanwhile, Ether and XRP both slid more than 5%. Brought to markets were also down, with the S&P 500 index slipping nearly 2%, during that same time frame. To talk more about markets, CNBC's Liz, Naples, Otano caught up with Rick Edelman, the Digital Assets Council of Financial Professionals, to get his take on recent price moves. So Bitcoin this week is trading above the $70,000 level. This is comes as the Iran war, concerns about it have eased, and some of Trump's comments earlier this week, I'm wondering what you make of Bitcoin trading in the same direction as other risk on assets, like equities. This kind of goes against one of the main use cases for Bitcoin that we've seen touted by some of its proponents, as this kind of hedge against geopolitical risk. What do you make of that? I think it's a valid observation, Liz, that as Bitcoin gets more and more mature, meaning as it becomes more mainstream, as there's greater adoption, not only among retail investors, but among institutional investors, it's becoming regarded as in the tech category, and it's therefore moving more in line with the stock market, particularly emerging markets, technology stocks, growth assets, risk assets, etc. That's a healthy good sign. It demonstrates that it's a mainstream asset, it's going to be treated as such. Bitcoin's predominant use these days is as a store of value. The notion of Satoshi way back in 2009 that it was going to be a new digital currency replacing Fiat currencies, that experiment has failed, that's over, nobody thinks Bitcoin is ever going to have that role. The use of Bitcoin as a transactional tool, being able to move money around the world, that's also been supplanted by stablecoins, and so Bitcoin's claim to fame is now twofold. Number one, store of value, and second, it has the biggest best brand in the world of crypto. It still has the number one market share by a huge amount, and whenever anybody anywhere expresses interest in investing in this asset class, Bitcoin is their first stop. It's how people begin to get engaged in this asset, and for that reason alone, Bitcoin is widely considered to have staying power, more so than other digital assets. I think your observation is valid, and it's going to demonstrate the mainstreaming of the permanency of this asset class. Now you talk about Bitcoin as a store of value, would you still say it's a hedge against inflation? Well, sure, like any other store of value, but that doesn't mean that it tracks inflation identically, it isn't correlated to inflation particularly. The biggest thing about Bitcoin, unlike all other asset classes, is it's incredibly low adoption rate so far. Less than 5% of the world owns Bitcoin. If you look at other asset classes, stocks, bonds, real estate, oil, precious metals, the adoption rate is dramatically higher, but Bitcoin is a long way to go, and that's a big reason why proponents argue we're in the very early innings of Bitcoin's pricing, because as there's greater adoption, you're going to have dramatic price increases because there's a fixed supply, unlike any other asset, except maybe real estate, you have an unlimited supply elsewhere. That's not going to prove to be the case with Bitcoin, and that's a big reason why so many are so bullish about the future price. Now you talk about adoption, you're a big proponent of Bitcoin adoption. You crypto more widely correct, so you recently, I think, within the past year or so, you are advising individuals to allocate somewhere between 10% for more conservative investors to 40% of the portfolios to crypto. Now that the market's pulled back, Bitcoin is more than 30% off its record high of 126,000 ish hit late in mid-October of last year, would you still give that same recommendation? Over and much so. If you'd loved it at 126, you'd have to be ecstatic about it at 70. So the reason that I argue for Bitcoin having 10% to 40% allocations is twofold. Number one, we have to recognize that adoption is growing, and that means Bitcoin's returns are very likely to dramatically outperform any other asset class. We talk about five or 10% returns for other assets. Bitcoin is going to be 5X or 10X over the next five to 10 years. So the profit potential is massive. The second reason that we need to have a serious allocation to crypto is because of longevity. We're living longer than ever before. We know this, and it's going to continue, thanks to medical innovation and technology, which means odds are really good, according to scientists who study this, that if you're alive in 2030, you're going to live to age 100 or beyond. That means the 60-40 portfolio model, where you begin to reduce your equity exposure in your 60s and 70s, is obsolete. 60-40 is thrown out, we are replacing it with 80-20, which means you have to have more of your money and equities for much longer in your life. And if that's going to be true, if you're going to have 70, 80% of your money and equities, crypto needs to be a much stronger allocation than just a 1 or 2%. It needs to be 10 or 15 or 20% for most investors. And as people begin to realize that and adopt it, that's going to further fuel the inflows into this asset class, which will result in further price increases. OK, let's talk about the top stories. Binance is suing the Wall Street Journal over claims of defamation. In a complaint filed in New York federal court today, the crypto exchange argues that the journal published a quote, false and defamatory article in February 23rd. That story claims Binance, quote, dismantled a staff investigation into $1 billion that had recently moved through Binance to a network funding around backed terror groups. Another report cited company documents and sources familiar with Binance's operations. The journal's report claims a trading account belonging to a close Binance business partner was identified as a primary channel to move the cryptocurrency in the exchange, quote, subsequently, fired the investigators who had uncovered the transfers and the network remained active. Now a Binance spokesperson told the journal that investigators weren't suspended or terminated for raising compliance concerns and in today's lawsuit, the company says it launched the compliance investigation as a result of law enforcement requests and also conducted an independent investigation that ended in off-boarding user accounts it says engaged in suspicious activity. Finance said in the complaint that it did not terminate personnel for any reporting or role in the investigations. We reached out to the Wall Street Journal but haven't heard back yet. Next, Wells Fargo may soon offer new crypto services. The banking giant moved to trademark the term WFUSD which would cover a range of crypto-related activities. Potential products or services mentioned on the trademark application include crypto hardware wallets, crypto trading, and staking, as well as blockchain-based systems. The other major trad-fi players have also been ramping up their crypto efforts. JP Morgan told CMBC over the summer it was developing a stablecoin-like deposit token of JPMD. One other thing we're watching over the last week federal regulators issued new guidance to loosen rules around tokenized securities. Banking regulators include the Federal Reserve and FDIC clarified last Thursday that banks shouldn't have to hold extra capital against securities that are tokenized on the blockchain. They've announced basically it's capital parity. In other words, tokenized securities should be treated like normal securities and the fact that they're issued in a different ledger technology, etc. That's not necessarily means that from an accounting perspective, they need to be treated differently. I think this compliments very well what the SEC announced a few months back that tokenized securities are securities and what they're doing now is just confirming that from an accounting perspective how it's treated is to be also the same and that there is no need to treat them differently that the fact that they are issued a new ledger technology that have smart contracts, etc. That's not in to use any additional risk for having to have higher capital reserves. When you deal with tokenized securities, it's supposed to traditional bookend to securities. Wall Street and crypto firms have been ramping up their adoption of tokenized assets in recent months as US crypto regulation takes shape. I think the last since November last year with the change of administration and then the new appointment of the new SEC chair, Paul Utkins and the creation of the crypto task force, I think we've seen a tremendous amount of progress in terms of regulation towards tokenized securities. As I mentioned, one of the fundamental things that the SEC said is that tokenized securities are equal to securities and therefore the fact that their issue on permissionless decentralized networks doesn't change the nature of the asset. That's very important because it clarifies the regulatory situation of the securities. They've also allowed broker dealers to do custody of tokenized securities without requiring a separate license as we had before in the previous administration. Now we have the accounting treatment of tokenized securities, being at parity with normal securities, so we've also, as you've seen, announced integration with defied trading protocols. That doesn't really require any regulatory change, but the fact that we're doing it and it's out there for the regulators to review, I think that's an important step forward. So I think at this point in time, there's very little left except more adoption and more market participants coming into the space, but the amount of progress we've done in the last year has been tremendous. Okay, that's all for CryptoWorld this week, but we'll be back again next Wednesday and we'll see you then.
